Tesla Is Pulling the Plug on the Cybertruck and the Internet Got the Party Started
62 photos
Photo: Tesla
The end of an ERROR. Not an era, but an ERROR. This is how the internet is defining the moment Tesla announced that it is winding down production of what was its first and might be its last pickup truck. Rest in peace, Cybertruck. You have been unloved, and probably, you won’t be missed.
Elon Musk officially announced that Tesla is pulling the plug on the Cybertruck , with production at Gigafactory Texas ending by mid-2027 to free up manufacturing capacity for the self-driving Cybercab robotaxi. The decision marks a swift end to one of the most polarizing experiments in modern automotive history.
Because that is exactly what the Cybertruck has been: an experiment that tricked the market with the wow factor before demand slowed down and completely collapsed. Driven onto the stage in Los Angeles in late November 2019. While Tesla promised it would be bulletproof, chief design Franz von Holzhausen, accidentally shattered two windows on the prototype during its live unveiling.
Elon Musk got up on stage to promise the Cybertruck would go into production by 2021, with a starting price of $39,900. However, the long-awaited EV started out in life as one more example of Musk overpromising and underdelivering.
Photo: Tesla It was a "baby" born after a four-year-long labour. The EV didn't go into production until the summer of 2023, with the first ten deliveries taking place at the factory later that year, on November 30. From that moment on, the market went crazy. Everyone wanted a piece of the Cybertruck. That is the effect of low production numbers.
Sellers couldn't care less about the resale ban It happened with the Cybertruck, and it is happening now with the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X. Earlier today, autoevolution brought to you the $696,445 ZR1X, listed for sale with a $400,000 markup by a dealership in Arkansas.
While many customers waited for their turn to get their hands on a Cybertruck right off the factory floor, even more tried to snatch one on the used car market. Despite the resale clause that banned customers from reselling their trucks during the first year of ownership, the market was flooded with Cybertrucks.
But the market was also flooded with backlash and drama. A Porsche dealership in Orlando paid $244,000 to buy a Cybertruck. Days later, it relisted the EV for sale for a mind-blowing $289,999. Just keep in mind that the Foundation Series started at $99,990 for the Dual-Motor All-Wheel Drive variant and $119,990 for the tri-motor Cyberbeast.
Photo: Tesla Yet, no sign of Elon Musk’s $39,900 truck promised back in 2019. Tesla did roll out a single-motor, rear-wheel-drive Cybertruck in April 2025, but it started at $69,990. It was a short-lived glory (or make that disaster?) for the rear-wheel-drive entry-level Cybertruck. Tesla sold only 173 units and retired it in mid-September due to low demand. So much for making the Cybertruck affordable.
The beginning of the end From that moment on, it was the beginning of the end for the Cybertruck that did not even float, as Elon Musk promised at some point. In the meantime, Tesla and SpaceX sent the Roadster flying, but the Cybertruck is not even watertight, as customers complained of water intrusion in the cargo bed just as often as they complained about the huge windshield wiper failing or interior pillar trim coming off.
However, every cloud has a silver lining, and the Cybertruck came with its own. Many owners bragged about how FSD has simplified their lives, sparing them the trouble of driving the truck themselves. The power and speed were also something they have very much enjoyed.
The Cybertruck Cyberbeast arrived with supercar numbers and performance . Its tri-motor setup produces 845 horsepower (857 metric horsepower) and 864 pound-feet (1,171 Newton meters) of torque. The zero-tailpipe-emission truck flashes from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in 2.6 seconds, runs the quarter mile in 11.0 seconds, and tops out at 130 mph (209 kph).
Photo: Tesla While Elon Musk had promised a range of 500 miles (805 kilometers) from the stainless steel "fridge on wheels," the best the 123-kWh battery pack could do was 350 miles (563 kilometers) in the retired Cybertruck RWD.
The end of an era error
As Tesla announced the demise of the Cybertruck, the internet is already dancing on its grave, calling the moment "The end of an ERROR" and saying they won’t be missing it. Underneath Musk's original X announcement, top replies mocked the financial math, pointing out the massive R&D spend versus roughly 70,000 lifetime sales, while others joked about having to go back to roasting traditional pickup trucks. In the meantime, the Cybertruck once again got unwanted publicity, being called a "recycle bin."
On Instagram, users joked that Tesla still has a 500-unit stockpile of unsold vehicles "to satisfy demand, perhaps for a thousand years." While the backlash goes on and on, it turns out that not everyone hated the Cybertruck.
Some call it "the best Tesla that ever was" and praise it for the advanced tech, power, and speed. Who can blame them? Now that the Tesla Cybertruck is on its way out, the only high-performance electric trucks on the market will be the GMC Hummer EV Pickup Truck with 1,160 horsepower nd the Rivian R1T with 1,025 horsepower. Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 6, 2026
